segments.note: The all-rail PRR Main Line opened Feb 15, 1854 via the new Horseshoe Curve, cutting the Philadelphia-Pittsburgh trip from ~4 days to ~15 hours. It replaced the state-owned 'Main Line of Public Works' (1834-1857ish): a mixed canal-and-inclined-plane system (Philadelphia & Columbia Railroad, two canal divisions, and the 10-plane Allegheny Portage Railroad over the mountains) that PRR bought from Pennsylvania in 1857 and continued using for freight into the early 1900s. Frequency on the new rail route in these early decades is estimated, unsourced.

properties.line: Pennsylvania Railroad: New York – Washington (Northeast Corridor)
properties.speed_source: estimated/blended across the line's history: ~20 km/h in the fragmented, ferry-broken 1838-73 era, rising to 90+ km/h for the electrified Congressional Limited by the 1930s-60s; unsourced

segments.note: No single railroad yet connected New York and Washington. A through trip meant chaining three independent companies and two ferry crossings: the Camden & Amboy (New York-area boat to South Amboy, rail to Camden, opposite Philadelphia) reached full Bordentown-Camden operation in 1834; the Philadelphia, Wilmington & Baltimore completed Philadelphia-Baltimore by Jan 1838 (with a steam-ferry break over the Susquehanna at Havre de Grace/Perryville until an 1866 bridge); and the B&O's Washington Branch opened Baltimore-Washington Aug 25, 1835. 1838 is when the last piece of this chain came together. Frequency is a rough estimate for the multi-carrier, multi-transfer trip, not a real timetable.
sources: Segment-level: this segment's own note carries the citation for its dates and service. Supporting references for the line:

segments.note: Pennsylvania Railroad, which had leased the United New Jersey Railroad & Canal Co. (successor to the Camden & Amboy) in 1871, built its own Baltimore & Potomac Railroad into Washington (bypassing the B&O, via the new B&P Tunnel under Baltimore) and struck a through-running agreement with the PW&B, giving unified if still PRR-branded service starting 1873. Trains still terminated at Jersey City, requiring a ferry across the Hudson to Manhattan. PRR bought the PW&B outright in 1881 (fully merged into the PRR mainline by 1902). Frequency estimated.

segments.note: PRR completed electrification of the entire New York-Washington line in 1935 (GG1 locomotives, the Congressional Limited and other fast all-electric trains), the busiest and fastest passenger corridor in the US for decades. Amtrak assumed the route May 1, 1971; it continues today as the core of the Northeast Corridor (see amtrak.geojson's Northeast Regional/Acela entries for the modern service). Frequency estimated at this era's peak.

segments.note: Amtrak inherited the Broadway Limited (NY-Philadelphia-Harrisburg-Pittsburgh-Chicago) on May 1, 1971, without interruption from PRR/Penn Central. It initially ran combined with the National Limited (NY-St Louis) as far as Pittsburgh; from July 12, 1971 the National Limited split off as its own train sharing this Harrisburg-Pittsburgh trackage until its discontinuation Oct 1, 1979. Aggregate frequency on this stretch estimated at ~2 round trips/day across the two trains.

segments.note: Replaced the Broadway Limited on Sept 10, 1995 running NY-Philadelphia-Pittsburgh-Chicago, daily 1 round trip. Discontinued March 7, 2005 amid Amtrak budget cuts, ending regular long-distance NY-Chicago service via the ex-PRR Main Line. Amtrak's shorter Philadelphia-Pittsburgh Pennsylvanian (see amtrak.geojson, running since 1980) has continued to serve this corridor since.
